summary: This paper proves the existence of a two-dimensional quantum system with local, translation-invariant, time-independent interactions that autonomously corrects quantum errors and performs universal computation without measurements or external control. The construction uses a dissipative quantum cellular automaton whose self-simulating structure implements a hierarchical concatenated code with Toom's rule protecting the control layer, and a nonzero noise threshold is established below which logical errors are suppressed exponentially with system size.
motivation: Passive quantum error correction has been ruled out in two dimensions under conventional stabilizer Hamiltonian assumptions, but active schemes require external measurements and classical processing. Understanding whether truly autonomous quantum error correction and computation can be achieved in physically realistic two-dimensional systems addresses a fundamental question in quantum information theory.
method: The scheme combines: (1) a universal quantum cellular automaton ($\mathsf{Univ}$) that simulates arbitrary local dynamics via a product-state program; (2) measurement-free concatenated quantum error correction with fault-tolerant gadget sets; (3) Toom's classical cellular automaton rule applied to local structure registers storing space-time coordinates $(\tau, x, y)$; and (4) self-simulation where the system encodes its own transition rule in the initial state, enabling recursive hierarchical correction. Noise is modeled as local faults at each update location with strength $\eta$, and the threshold proof uses the extended-rectangle formalism tracking damage sets that shrink geometrically under fault-free evolution.
result: For local noise strength $\eta < \eta_{\mathrm{th}}$ (a nonzero constant threshold), a circuit of depth $D$ on $N$ qubits is simulated to accuracy $\delta$ using $\mathcal{O}(N \, \mathrm{polylog}(ND/\delta))$ physical qudits and runtime $\mathcal{O}(D \, \mathrm{polylog}(ND/\delta))$ with $\mathcal{O}(\log\log(ND/\delta))$ encoding levels; memory lifetime diverges in the thermodynamic limit. A continuous-time implementation using a time-independent local Lindbladian with engineered dissipative jump operators achieves the same threshold.
